exam-10-q01.why_correct_en: The patron Saint of England is St George.

exam-10-q02.why_correct_en: Loch Lomond and the Trossachs National Park is located in the west of Scotland.

exam-10-q03.why_correct_en: False. An established church is a church given a special constitutional and legal relationship with the state; this does not mean that Wales or Northern Ireland has no Christian churches. Wales was once part of the Church of England's diocesan structure. By the nineteenth century, however, many Welsh Christians belonged to Nonconformist churches while the Anglican Church retained its official position. The Welsh Church Act 1914 took effect in 1920, when the Church in Wales was disestablished and became a self-governing Anglican province. In Ireland, the established Protestant Church of Ireland was widely resented because most of the population was Roman Catholic. The Irish Church Act 1869 disestablished it from 1871, and it was not re-established in Northern Ireland after partition.

exam-10-q04.why_correct_en: Geoffrey Chaucer wrote a series of poems in English about a group of people going to Canterbury on a pilgrimage. This collection of poems is called The Canterbury Tales.

exam-10-q05.why_correct_en: Boxing Day is the day after Christmas Day (26th December) and is a public holiday.

exam-10-q06.why_correct_en: There are public holidays each year called bank holidays, when banks and many other businesses are closed for the day.

exam-10-q07.why_correct_en: In 1918, women over the age of 30 were given voting rights and the right to stand for Parliament, partly in recognition of the contribution women made to the war effort during the First World War.

exam-10-q08.why_correct_en: In the UK, you must have a driving licence to drive on public roads.

exam-10-q09.why_correct_en: The Edinburgh Festival takes place in Edinburgh, Scotland, every summer. It is a series of different arts and cultural festivals, with the biggest and most well-known being the Edinburgh Festival Fringe (‘the Fringe’).

exam-10-q10.why_correct_en: There are 60 members of the Welsh government or members of the Senedd (SMs) and elections are held every four years using a form of proportional representation.

exam-10-q11.why_correct_en: False. Members of the public are not allowed in Youth Courts, and the name or photographs of the accused young person cannot be published in newspapers or used by the media.

exam-10-q12.why_correct_en: Sir Edward Elgar (1857-1934) was a musician. His best known work is probably the Pomp and Circumstance Marches. March No1 (Land of Hope and Glory) is usually played at the Last Night of the Proms at the Royal Albert Hall.

exam-10-q13.why_correct_en: There are no £25 notes in the UK.

exam-10-q14.why_correct_en: The Scottish Grand National takes place at Ayr.

exam-10-q15.why_correct_en: The laws passed after the Glorious Revolution marked the beginning of the constitutional monarchy.

exam-10-q16.why_correct_en: Elizabeth I became one of the most popular monarchs in English history, particularly after 1588, when the English defeated the Spanish Armada (a large fleet of ships), which had been sent by Spain to conquer England and restore Catholicism.

exam-10-q17.why_correct_en: The Habeas Corpus Act became law in 1679. This was a very important piece of legislation which remains relevant today. Habeas corpus is Latin for ‘you must present the person in court’. The Act guaranteed that no one could be held prisoner unlawfully. Every prisoner has a right to a court hearing.

exam-10-q18.why_correct_en: Emmeline Pankhurst she set up the women’s Franchise League in 1889, which fought to get the vote in local elections for married women. In 1903 she helped found the Women’s Social and Political Union (WSPU). This was the first group whose members were called ‘suffragettes’. The group used civil disobedience as part of their protest to gain the vote for women. In 1918, women over the age of 30 were given voting rights and the right to stand for Parliament, partly in recognition of the contribution women made to the war effort during the First World War.

exam-10-q19.why_correct_en: The Proms is an eight-week summer season of orchestral classical music that takes place in various venues, including the Royal Albert Hall in London.

exam-10-q20.why_correct_en: Newton‘s most famous published work was Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica (‘Mathematical Principle of Natural Philosophy’), which showed how gravity applied to the whole universe.

exam-10-q21.why_correct_en: The World War I ended in 1918.

exam-10-q22.why_correct_en: The Emperor Hadrian built a wall in the north of England to keep out the Picts (ancestors of the Scottish people).

exam-10-q23.why_correct_en: Rowing is also popular, both as a leisure activity and as a competitive sport. There is a popular yearly race on the Thames between Oxford and Cambridge Universities.

exam-10-q24.why_correct_en: The British constitution is not written down in any single document, and therefore it is described as ‘unwritten’.
